body.p: Applicant responds to the final Office Action dated June 13, 2024, and requests the Examiner consider the following remarks.

The Examiner asserts that since "Columns 2-3, lines 64-7 of Huber (984) [teaches] it is disclosed that there can be an almost infinite number of configurations of the ball-mat contours and openings due to the building-block systems by connecting the side profiles with corner pieces, which could easily be formed to extend throughout a cargo compartment" that it would be obvious to extend the "ball mat contours" of Huber (984) "from the forward end of the cargo compartment, through the forward section, through the entranceway section, and through the aft section to the aft end." Applicant disagrees and does not see how this logically follows. Huber (984) teaches "[a] ball matfor the loading deck of an aircraft..." (Emphasis added, Abstract). One skilled in the art would have no such motivation to extend a ball mat structure outside the loading deck area. First, it would add unnecessary weight, which is a significant consideration in aviation technology. Second, there are no ball transfer units away from the loading deck, which with the ball mat is designed to interact. Accordingly, Applicant requests reconsideration of the prior arguments in light of the above.

The Examiner goes on to assert "it would have been a mere matter of design choice to make the different portions of the ball mat of whatever form or shape was desired or expedient. A change in form or shape is generally recognized as being within the level of ordinary skill in the art, absent showing of unexpected results. In re Dailey et al., 149 USPQ 47." Id. In re Dailey is non-analogous to the present case. MPEP 2144.04 states "[a]s discussed in MPEP 2144, an examiner may utilize legal precedent as a source of supporting rationale when warranted and appropriately supported. In formulating any rejection invoking legal precedent, the Examiner must take care to ensure that the rational is explained and shown to apply to the facts at hand" (emphasis added). Here, the legal precedent cited by the Examiner does not apply to the facts at hand. In particular, In re Daily held that the shape of an element of a claimed disposable plastic nursing container was a matter of choice which a person of ordinary skill in the art would have found obvious absent persuasive evidence that the particular configuration of the claimed container was significant. There, claims 27 and 28 were considered "a 'mere matter of choice'

not significantly novel over Matzen" (Id. at 1034). "Claim 27, while defining no particular nipple opening structure, recites the configuration of the top and bottom sections of the container as that of 'a portion of a sphere less than a hemisphere' [i.e., a shape]. In claim 28, the central angle of those spherical portions is about 80 degrees [i.e., a shape]." (Id. at 1031). Accordingly, (1) claims 27 and 28 were explicitly directed towards a shape of the claimed invention; and (2) the modification of the shape was the only change to the prior art reference. Here, in contrast, the claim limitation "the plurality of trays are continuously covered from the forward end of the cargo compartment, through the forward section, through the entranceway section, and through the aft section to the aft end" is not a mere significant shape change over the prior art, and the Examiner is utilizing two references Huber (462) and Huber (984) plus the modified shape, not just a single reference and the modified shape.

More specifically, "the plurality of trays [being] continuously covered from the forward end of the cargo compartment, through the forward section, through the entranceway section, and through the aft section to the aft end" is not a "mere matter of design choice" analogous to "a change of shape" of a single feature as the only modification of a reference. The limitation is not taught by either reference, and there is no rationale for one skilled in the art to make such a modification. Furthermore, assuming arguendo that In re Daily is relevant, the configuration is significant. More specifically, as recited in the background section, "[c]argo handling systems, such as those used by aircraft for transport of containerized cargo or pallets, also referred to as unit load devices (ULDs), typically include longitudinal trays containing transport rollers positioned along a cargo deck floor to facilitate movement of the ULDs relative to the deck floor. The space between the longitudinal trays is typically filled with floor panels to provide a walking surface. In typical cargo handling systems, the longitudinal trays may be trip hazards for personnel walking through a cargo compartment" (emphasis added, [0003]). In this regard, covering the plurality of trays as claimed prevents this trip hazard and is a significant aspect of the presently claimed invention.

Furthermore, neither Huber reference teaches this limitation. First, Huber (984) has no trays, and Huber (462) does not have trays that are "continuously covered from the forward end of the cargo compartment, through the forward section, through the entranceway section, and through the aft section to the aft end." Furthermore, as outlined below, Huber (984) does not even teach that the trays are "continuously covered" in the entranceway section. Accordingly,
such a modification would not be a mere "matter of design choice" as asserted by the Examiner.

The Examiner rejects claims 1-10, 15, 16, 18, and 21-24 under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. Patent No. 7,556,462 ('462 Huber) in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,125,984 ('984 Huber). Applicant respectfully disagrees and traverses the rejection.

Applicant believes the Examiner is misconstruing the Huber (462) reference. In particular, nowhere in Huber is it disclosed or contemplated that the trays 10 are continuously covered in any manner. The Examiner states that "Figure 1: Shows the topskin composed over a plurality of trays (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3) to create a conveying area of the workpieces (area by door region 55), and is covered over the entirety of the trays in the conveying section." This is incorrect. FIG. 1 shows the sidewalls of the trays extending longitudinally through the cargo deck from one end to the other end uncovered. The view is a top down view and the elements of the ball mat 21 are shown as being disposed between the sidewalls of the trays (10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3).

This is further evidenced by FIG. 2, which shows the "the central mounting profile 10 is shown in front view as well as two containers 1, 2 with their edge profiles 5, 6 resting on external rollers 31, 32 that extend outward from the mounting profile 10." Accordingly, elements 5, 6 in FIG. 2 are components of the containers 1, 2 that are being loaded into the cargo deck and there is no "topskin" that is covering the "tray 10" that is shown.

FIG. 1 of Huber (462) actually corresponds to the problem that the presently claimed invention is solving. More specifically, the background of the present disclosure states "[t]he space between the longitudinal trays is typically filled with floor panels to provide a walking surface" (emphasis added). Similarly, the ball mats 21 in Huber (462) are disposed between, not continuously over, the trays as shown in FIG. 1 of Huber (462). Accordingly, the trays of Huber (462) would remain a trip hazard for personnel walking through a cargo compartment" (Present Disclosure, [0003]). Nowhere in Huber (462) is it disclosed that the ball mats 21 cover the trays, nor does FIG. 1 support this position. More specifically, as shown in annotated FIG. 1 below, the sidewalls of the trays 10, 10-1, 10-2, 10-3 remain solid from the top down view from one end of the cargo deck to the other end of the cargo deck through the section with ball mats 21. The ball mats 21 are illustrated as being between, not disposed over, the trays 10. Furthermore, nowhere in
the specification of Huber (462) is it disclosed or contemplated that the ball mats "cover" the trays

Furthermore, the trays of Huber (984) are also not "continuously covered" as claimed, which further provides evidence that Huber (462) does not teach "continuously cover[ing]" the trays with ball mats. In particular, as shown in annotated FIG. 2 below from Huber (984), the flange A of the tray is flush with the mat B (compare with A' and B' of FIG. 5B from the Present Disclosure annotated below), not "continuously covered" by the mat B.

In conclusion, neither Huber (984) or Huber (462) disclose, contemplate, or render obvious at least "a topskin disposed on and mated to the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface of the first tray, the topskin further coupled to the first top mating surface and the second top mating surface of the second tray, wherein: the first tray and the second tray are disposed entirely below the topskin, and the plurality of trays are continuously covered from the forward end of the cargo compartment, through the forward section, through the entranceway section, and through the aft section to the aft end" as recited in independent claim 1 and similarly recited in independent claims 8 and 14.

Accordingly, Applicant asserts that Huber (984) and Huber (462) fail to render obvious independent claims 1, 8, and 15 as recited herein. Therefore, Applicant asserts that the rejection should be withdrawn.

In view of the above remarks, Applicant respectfully submits that all pending claims are allowable and requests allowance of the pending claims. The Examiner is invited to telephone the undersigned at the Examiner's convenience, if that would help further prosecution of the subject application. Applicant authorizes and respectfully requests that any fees due or overpayments be charged or credited to Deposit Account No. 19-2814. This statement does NOT authorize payment of the issue fee.
Respectfully submitted,
